summary: Describes an abstract mechanism by which senders tell the network about congestion recently experienced by packets in their flow, so network elements can see the congestion as well as the receiver.

plainLanguage.summary: ConEx lets a sender report congestion signals it has received in packets sent back through the network. RFC 7713 describes the mechanism and requirements, but leaves concrete encodings to other specifications.

questions: how does conex help networks manage traffic
why do senders need to report congestion
how can a network audit conex signals
subtitle: An abstract mechanism for exposing congestion information in IP packets

tldr.problem: Receivers report loss or ECN congestion signals to senders, but network devices cannot see what congestion a sender has experienced across the full path.
tldr.mechanism: A ConEx-capable sender reflects congestion feedback in IP-layer signals. Network devices can observe the signals, and audit mechanisms can check that they do not understate congestion.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7713 defines an abstract mechanism and requirements, not packet formats or a complete protocol specification.

facts.label: Minimum signal delay
facts.value: At least one round-trip time in the general case

today: RFC 7713 is an Informational abstract-mechanism document and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It does not specify packet formats or codepoint allocations.

sections.title: What ConEx Exposes
sections.content:
Network devices signal congestion by dropping packets or marking them with Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN). The receiver returns this information to the sender through transport feedback, and the sender adjusts its behavior. Those signals are not otherwise visible to every IP-layer device on the forward path.

Congestion Exposure (ConEx) adds an IP-layer signal that lets a sender relay information about congestion encountered earlier in the same flow. Network policy devices may use it for monitoring or traffic management. This RFC describes an abstract mechanism and does not define a complete protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: ConEx lets a sender put information about earlier congestion into packets traveling through the network. Network devices along the path can read that information.

sections.title: The ConEx Signal Types
sections.content:
A ConEx signal is carried in a packet sent by a ConEx-capable transport. Re-Echo-Loss reports that the transport experienced packet loss. Re-Echo-ECN reports that it detected an ECN Congestion Experienced mark. Credit signals advance notice of risk that packets may contribute to congestion.

ConEx-Not-Marked indicates that a transport is ConEx-capable but is not sending a loss, ECN, or Credit signal in that packet. The document requires concrete specifications to state the units used for congestion, such as bytes or packets, and to explain the consequences of that choice.
sections.plainLanguage: ConEx signals can report loss, ECN marking, or credit for possible future congestion. A concrete protocol must define how it counts congestion.

sections.title: Possible Encodings and Their Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The RFC describes several example encodings without assigning specific bits or codepoints. A naive encoding marks retransmissions and ECN-related reductions, but it does not support auditing. A null encoding infers congestion from TCP headers in limited circumstances. An ECN-based encoding combines ConEx with ECN information.

Other examples use independent flag bits or one of a set of codepoints for Not-ConEx, ConEx-Not-Marked, Re-Echo-Loss, Re-Echo-ECN, and Credit. The document treats these as design options, because each encoding has different limits and possible effects on auditability.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC compares several ways a protocol might represent ConEx signals. It leaves the exact packet encoding for other specifications to decide.

sections.title: Senders, Policy Devices, and Auditors
sections.content:
ConEx requires modified senders to produce signals. Receivers may not need changes if their transport feedback is sufficient; TCP loss feedback is sufficient when SACK is used, while more precise TCP ECN feedback may be useful. Existing network devices can continue to signal congestion through loss or ECN.

Policy devices may monitor markings and take actions such as policing, rerouting, or changing service class. Auditors check whether ConEx signals understate actual congestion. The RFC discusses ECN auditing, TCP-specific loss auditing, and auditing at a predominant bottleneck, and notes that accurate loss auditing is not generally possible in every network.
sections.plainLanguage: Senders need to add ConEx signals. Network policy devices can monitor them, while auditors compare them with congestion evidence to detect underreporting.

sections.title: Incremental Deployment and Security
sections.content:
ConEx is intended to work under partial deployment. Packets can indicate whether they are ConEx-capable, so unmodified senders can continue to send ordinary packets. Receivers and forwarding devices generally need no ConEx-specific changes, although some transports may benefit from more precise feedback.

The main security concern identified is that senders may understate congestion to avoid policy consequences. The RFC calls for audit mechanisms and sufficient sanctions, but says concrete protocol specifications need their own security analysis. It does not standardize an audit function.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks and senders can adopt ConEx in stages. A concrete protocol still needs to define how it audits signals and addresses attempts to underreport congestion.
